content.thinking:
This looks like a social-norm intervention using a slider estimate followed by corrective feedback about public trust in climate scientists, since people tend to underestimate that trust. I'm reasoning that descriptive norm effects on personal attitudes are typically modest but genuine, so I'd expect a moderate boost of around +2 to +3 points in multidimensional trust, especially given the interactive surprise element strengthens the effect.

I'm settling on trust_multidimensional around +2.1 to +2.2, with anchoring shrinking the more direct trust_post to about +1.9 and distrust_post dropping around -1.5. Funding perceptions, policy role, and institutional trust see smaller diluted gains near +0.7 to +1.0, while behavioral outcomes like donations and newsletter signups stay minimal. I'm also weighing that revealing "23% had little or no trust" could partly cue distrust, but the net effect should still be positive given the pro-social consensus framing.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is an interactive descriptive-norm correction: respondents first guess the share of Americans who trust climate scientists (Americans systematically underestimate such pro-science norms, especially in a perceived-polarized context), then receive a credible Pew correction (76% at least some trust). The mechanism is social proof/consensus-of-peers plus a mild depolarization frame, which is proximal to the trust construct itself and benefits from the surprise/self-generated-error format, so I place it modestly above the average arm on the primary trust battery (~+2.2 points, d≈0.09). The re-asked single items (trust_post, belief_post) are anchored by pre-treatment measurement, so I shrink them relative to the fresh multidimensional battery; distrust gets a smaller-magnitude negative because the text also mentions the 23% who distrust, which partially cues the opposing norm. Downstream constructs (funding, scientists' policy role, institutional trust) get sub-point-to-1-point effects since trust is only an indirect input, and belief/concern/policy/behavioral intentions get well under 1 point because nothing in the text presents climate evidence or risk information. Incentivized outcomes are near zero: a few cents on the $10 donation and about a percentage point on newsletter sign-up.
